entries.context: Post-Wave2 · algebra · associative ring with a multiplicative identity
entries.definition: A unital ring is an associative ring (R,+,·,0) equipped with an element 1_R such that 1_R·r=r=r·1_R for every r∈R. Multiplication is not required to be commutative. The zero ring, where 0=1_R, is included unless a nonzero-ring convention is stated.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Associativity is assumed for the underlying ring.
The zero ring is not excluded by this definition.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · algebra · identity-preserving ring homomorphism
entries.definition: For unital rings R and S, a unital ring homomorphism f:R→S is an additive map satisfying f(ab)=f(a)f(b) for all a,b∈R and f(1_R)=1_S. In particular f preserves 0. Some authors include preservation of 1 in the unqualified term 'ring homomorphism'; others do not.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Both source and target have designated multiplicative identities.
Explicit identity preservation distinguishes this convention from a nonunital homomorphism.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · category theory · smallness of morphism collections
entries.definition: A category C is locally small if, for every ordered pair of objects X,Y of C, the collection Hom_C(X,Y) of morphisms from X to Y is a set rather than a proper class (relative to the chosen foundational universe). Its collection of objects need not be a set. Every small category is locally small, but the converse need not hold.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: The set-versus-proper-class distinction is interpreted relative to a fixed foundational universe.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · commutative algebra · nonnegative integer grading (Stacks convention)
entries.definition: A nonnegatively graded (commutative, unital) ring S is a commutative unital ring together with an additive-group direct-sum decomposition S=⊕_{d≥0} S_d such that S_d·S_e⊆S_{d+e} for all d,e≥0. Every element of S is a finite sum of homogeneous elements. This is a nonnegative-integer grading; more general grading groups are separate conventions.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Commutative, unital-ring convention as in the cited Stacks Project section.
The grading is indexed by the nonnegative integers, not all integers or an arbitrary group.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · category theory · cofiltered indexing category
entries.definition: A category I is cofiltered if (1) it has at least one object; (2) for any objects x,y there is an object z with morphisms z→x and z→y; and (3) for any parallel morphisms a,b:x→y there are an object w and a morphism c:w→x such that a∘c=b∘c. Equivalently, the opposite category Iᵒᵖ is filtered.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: No smallness hypothesis is required for the abstract definition; small index categories are typical in use.
Condition (3) equalizes parallel arrows in the indexing category itself, not merely after applying an unrelated functor.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · geometry · affine torsor for a real vector space
aliases: affine space over the real numbers
entries.definition: A real affine space consists of a nonempty set A and a real vector space V whose additive group acts freely and transitively on A: for every a,b∈A there exists exactly one v∈V with a+v=b. No point of A is distinguished as an origin; choosing an origin identifies A with V, but not canonically.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: A is required to be nonempty, which follows automatically from the usual torsor convention.
Scalars are real; a corresponding definition over any field uses a vector space over that field.

entries.term: generating set of a left module
entries.context: Post-Wave2 · module theory · finite linear combination spanning
aliases: system of generators of a module
entries.definition: Let R be a unital ring and M a unital left R-module. A subset S⊆M generates M if every m∈M is a finite sum m=∑_{i=1}^n r_i s_i with r_i∈R and s_i∈S; equivalently, the smallest R-submodule containing S equals M. The empty subset generates precisely the zero module, using the empty sum 0.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · measure theory · finite measure in neighborhoods
aliases: locally finite measure on a Hausdorff space
entries.definition: Let X be a Hausdorff topological space and μ a nonnegative countably additive measure on the Borel σ-algebra B(X). The Borel measure μ is locally finite if every x∈X belongs to an open set U with μ(U)<∞. Then every compact K⊆X has finite μ-measure. Local finiteness alone does not imply inner or outer regularity.

entries.context: Homological algebra · degree-zero morphism of chain complexes
entries.definition: Let (C_n,d^C_n) and (D_n,d^D_n) be chain complexes in an additive category, with differentials decreasing degree by one. A chain map f:C_•→D_• is a family of morphisms f_n:C_n→D_n, one for each integer n, satisfying d^D_n∘f_n=f_{n−1}∘d^C_n for every n. Thus every square formed by f and the differentials commutes.

entries.context: Homological algebra · extension of homomorphisms from submodules
entries.definition: Let R be a unital ring and E a unital left R-module. The module E is injective if, whenever i:A→B is an injective homomorphism of left R-modules and f:A→E is R-linear, there exists an R-linear g:B→E with g∘i=f. Equivalently, the contravariant functor Hom_R(−,E) is exact on short exact sequences of left R-modules.

entries.context: General topology · open-set basis
entries.definition: For a topological space X, a collection B of subsets of X is a basis for its topology if every B∈B is open and, for every open U⊆X and every x∈U, there exists B∈B with x∈B⊆U. Equivalently, every open subset is a union of basis elements (the empty union gives ∅). The empty family is a basis when X is empty.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Basis here means basis of open sets, not a basis of a vector space.
Empty topological space and empty unions are included.

entries.context: General topology · open-set subbasis
entries.definition: For a topological space X, a family S of subsets of X is a subbasis if the family of all finite intersections of members of S (including the empty intersection X) is a basis for the topology. Equivalently, every open set is a union of finite intersections of elements of S. An empty subbasis generates the indiscrete topology {∅,X}.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Finite intersections include the empty intersection, interpreted as X.
The family S need not itself be closed under finite intersections.

entries.context: General topology · coinduced topology on a common target
aliases: strong topology induced by a family of maps
entries.definition: Let {X_i}_{i∈I} be topological spaces, Y a set, and f_i:X_i→Y set maps. The final topology on Y consists of precisely those U⊆Y for which f_i⁻¹(U) is open in X_i for every i∈I. It is the finest topology on Y making all f_i continuous; equivalently, g:Y→Z is continuous exactly when every composite g∘f_i is continuous, for any topological space Z.

entries.context: Analysis · topological support (closure of nonzero locus)
entries.definition: Let X be a topological space and f:X→V a function into an additive group V with zero 0. The (topological) support of f is supp(f)=cl_X({x∈X:f(x)≠0}), the closure of the set on which f is nonzero. Equivalently it is the smallest closed subset F⊆X such that f is identically zero on X∖F.

entries.context: Set theory and algebra · finite nonzero locus
entries.definition: Let X be a set and (V,0) a pointed set, for example an abelian group with its zero. A function f:X→V is finitely supported if the set {x∈X:f(x)≠0} is finite. The zero function has empty support. Here 'support' means the nonzero locus, without taking a topological closure; if X is a topological space with the discrete topology, its closure is the same set.

entries.context: Set theory · single-valued relation with possibly restricted domain
entries.definition: Given sets A and B, a partial function from A to B is a relation F⊆A×B such that for each a∈A there is at most one b∈B with (a,b)∈F. Its domain of definition is dom(F)={a∈A:∃b∈B,(a,b)∈F}; equivalently it is an ordinary function dom(F)→B, where dom(F)⊆A. It is total exactly when dom(F)=A.

entries.context: Linear algebra and geometry · affine codimension-one subspace
aliases: hyperplane in a real vector space
entries.definition: Let V be a real vector space. An affine hyperplane in V is a subset H={v∈V:ℓ(v)=c}, where ℓ:V→ℝ is a nonzero linear functional and c∈ℝ. Equivalently H=v₀+ker(ℓ) for any v₀∈H; it is a nonempty affine subspace whose direction subspace has codimension one. If V={0}, no affine hyperplane exists.

entries.term: formal power series ring in one variable
entries.context: Commutative algebra · one-indeterminate formal series ring
entries.definition: For a commutative unital ring R, the formal power series ring R[[T]] consists of all coefficient sequences (a_n)_{n≥0}, written symbolically ∑_{n≥0}a_nT^n. Addition is coefficientwise, and multiplication is the Cauchy product: the coefficient of T^n in fg is ∑_{k=0}^n a_kb_{n−k}. No analytic convergence or evaluation of T is assumed. The constant series 1_R is the multiplicative identity.

entries.term: bounded subset of a metric space
entries.context: Metric geometry · finite diameter subset
entries.definition: Let (X,d) be a metric space. A subset A⊆X is bounded if there exists a finite real M≥0 such that d(a,b)≤M for every a,b∈A. Equivalently, the diameter sup{d(a,b):a,b∈A} is finite when A is nonempty; boundedness also holds vacuously for A=∅. For nonempty X, this is equivalent to A lying in a ball of some finite radius about a point of X.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: A is permitted to be empty; the diameter of the empty set is left convention-dependent.
Boundedness depends on the specified metric, not only on the underlying topology.

entries.term: upper set of a partially ordered set
entries.context: Order theory · upward-closed subset
entries.definition: Let (P,≤) be a partially ordered set. A subset U⊆P is an upper set if, whenever x∈U and x≤y in P, it follows that y∈U. Both ∅ and P are upper sets. The principal upper set generated by p∈P is ↑p={y∈P:p≤y}. This is the order-dual notion to a lower set.

entries.context: Homological algebra · degree +1 homotopy between chain maps
entries.definition: Let f,g:C_•→D_• be chain maps between complexes in an additive category, with differentials lowering degree. A chain homotopy from f to g is a family of morphisms h_n:C_n→D_{n+1} satisfying f_n−g_n=d^D_{n+1}∘h_n+h_{n−1}∘d^C_n for every integer n. If such h exists then f and g are chain-homotopic.
assumptions: Works in any additive category; objects need not be modules.
In homological grading h raises degree by one; in cohomological grading a homotopy lowers degree by one.

entries.definition: A chain complex C_• in an abelian category is acyclic if H_n(C_•)=ker(d_n)/im(d_{n+1}) is the zero object for every n∈ℤ. Equivalently the sequence of differentials is exact at every degree: im(d_{n+1})=ker(d_n). Acyclicity alone does not imply that the complex is contractible.

entries.definition: Let R be a unital ring and M a unital left R-module. Injective hulls exist and are unique up to an isomorphism compatible with the inclusion of M.

entries.definition: A metric space (X,d) is totally bounded if, for every ε>0, there exist finitely many points x_1,…,x_n∈X such that X=⋃_{i=1}^n B_d(x_i,ε). For X=∅ one may take n=0. Equivalently, X admits a finite ε-net for every ε>0. Total boundedness implies boundedness, but not conversely.

entries.context: Algebra · multiplication- and identity-preserving mapping
entries.definition: For monoids (M,·,e_M) and (N,*,e_N), a monoid homomorphism f:M→N is a function satisfying f(x·y)=f(x)*f(y) for all x,y∈M and f(e_M)=e_N. Both conditions are needed in general: a semigroup homomorphism need not preserve monoid identities. In the standard convention, the adjective 'unital' simply emphasizes identity preservation already required of a monoid homomorphism.
assumptions: Both domain and codomain monoids have designated identities.
No commutativity or invertibility assumption.
Do not omit the identity equation.

entries.context: Measure theory and set theory · {0,1}-valued probability measure
entries.definition: On a measurable space (X,Σ), a two-valued countably additive probability measure is a function μ:Σ→{0,1} with μ(∅)=0, μ(X)=1, and μ(⋃_{n≥1}A_n)=∑_{n≥1}μ(A_n) for pairwise disjoint measurable A_n. On the full power set P(κ), the additional requirements μ({α})=0 for every α<κ (nonprincipal) and additivity across disjoint families of size <κ (κ-completeness) characterize the measure side of the usual measurable-cardinal definition. Mere countable additivity alone is not the same as κ-completeness for arbitrary κ.
assumptions: A specified σ-algebra for countable additivity.
No singleton nullity assumed for the general two-valued probability measure.
Cardinal application requires nonprincipality, domain P(κ), and κ-completeness; distinguish all these requirements.

entries.context: Differential equations · coefficients vary with independent variables
aliases: linear PDE operator with variable coefficients
entries.definition: For an open set Ω⊆ℝⁿ, a linear differential operator of order at most m with variable coefficients has the form Lu(x)=∑_{|α|≤m}a_α(x)∂^αu(x), where α ranges over multi-indices and coefficient functions a_α:Ω→𝔽 are prescribed independently of the unknown u. It is called variable-coefficient when at least one coefficient function is nonconstant; otherwise it has constant coefficients. Appropriate differentiability of u and regularity of a_α must be specified for a classical, weak, or distributional interpretation. Allowing dependence on u itself generally makes the operator nonlinear.

entries.term: weak topology of a CW complex
entries.context: Algebraic topology · final topology for cell characteristic maps
aliases: weak topology of a cell complex
entries.definition: Suppose X is a set equipped with a cellular decomposition and characteristic maps Φ_α:D^{n_α}→X whose interiors map homeomorphically onto disjoint open cells covering X. The weak topology relative to the cells is the final topology for these maps: a subset A⊆X is closed exactly when Φ_α⁻¹(A) is closed in D^{n_α} for every characteristic map. Equivalently, for a CW structure, A is closed if and only if A intersects the closure of every cell in a relatively closed set; it is also the direct-limit topology of the skeleta Xⁿ. This is not the weak topology σ(E,E*) of a topological vector space in functional analysis.

sources.title: Allen Hatcher — Algebraic Topology, Appendix: Topology of Cell Complexes

assumptions: Characteristic maps are part of the cellular structure; all cells cover X.
For the closure-of-cells description, assume the usual CW axioms, including closure-finiteness.
The term weak topology is mathematically ambiguous across algebraic topology and functional analysis.
